tldr: By repairing physical inconsistencies and compensating for missing actuation in high-dynamic martial arts motions extracted from monocular video, this work enables a real humanoid robot to execute acrobatic skills and recover from falls in about 0.7 s within a single unified policy—without any recovery reference data.
hero_caption: Overview of the framework. From a dataset of national-level martial artists' videos, the system repairs physical inconsistencies, applies low-kinetic-energy (LKE) sampling, and unifies dynamic motion tracking with ultra-fast fall recovery (approx. 0.7 s) and disturbance rejection into a single policy.
overview:
When trying to make humanoid robots perform acrobatic skills like backflips or jumping spins, the main bottleneck is motion data. Traditional motion capture (MoCap) requires expensive studio setups and specialized suits, making it tough to capture aggressive outdoor athletic movements. An obvious alternative is learning directly from web videos. However, simply retargeting video-reconstructed motions and running reinforcement learning fails completely.

Why does it fail? There are three main reasons. First, 3D poses reconstructed from monocular video are physically inconsistent: the robot floats in mid-air or penetrates into the ground (C1). Second, video carries no actuation or torque information; when a robot with different motor properties tries to strictly track the trajectory, it breaks down dynamically (C2). Third, videos show only successful executions without any failure or recovery scenes, leaving the robot helpless against disturbances (C3).

KungfuAthleteBot (KAB) tackles these three barriers head-on. It fixes jump trajectories using physics-guided parabolic trajectory correction and prevents learning failures from infeasible poses using a clever kinetic-energy-based initialization scheme (LKE sampling). On top of that, it unifies fall recovery and dynamic motion tracking inside a single policy. Tested on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, KAB successfully executes aggressive kung fu movements while demonstrating remarkable toughness—recovering from arbitrary falls in only about 0.7 seconds.
contributions: Constructed 'KungfuAthlete', a high-dynamic motion dataset featuring high linear and angular velocities derived from videos of national-level martial artists.
Introduced a physics-guided parabolic trajectory correction pipeline that repairs floating and ground penetration instead of discarding high-dynamic jump frames.

Developed pseudo-low-kinetic-energy (LKE) sampling, which biases initialization towards dynamically feasible, low-energy states rather than tracking error, compensating for missing torque information.
Achieved tracking of dynamic video motions, disturbance rejection, and recovery from arbitrary falls in approx. 0.7 s within a single unified policy without any recovery reference data.

sections.heading: The Three Barriers Humanoids Face When Learning from Video
sections.summary: Video data is abundant and cheap, but it suffers from three critical flaws for humanoid control: physical inconsistency, missing actuation information, and an absence of failure and recovery data. This work repairs and compensates for each flaw to achieve dynamic motion and ultra-fast recovery on a real humanoid.
sections.details:
When training humanoid robots for dynamic locomotion, conventional motion capture (MoCap) is constrained by physical setups and struggles to scale. Videos from platforms like YouTube offer a vast alternative, but piping them directly into a robot controller fails. The authors summarize the core issues into three points:

- (C1) Physical Inconsistency: Monocular pose estimators output motions with bodies floating in the air (failing to follow ballistic parabolas), penetrating the ground upon landing, and high-frequency jitter. Such floating root trajectories are physically impossible for a robot to track.
- (C2) Missing Actuation Information: Video pixels only show kinematic poses, revealing nothing about which joint generated what torque. Because humans and robots have very different torque limits and mass distributions, forcing strict trajectory tracking demands impossible joint efforts and stalls learning.
- (C3) Missing Failure and Recovery: Videos only capture successful executions, offering zero information on how to regain balance when pushed. The slightest real-world disturbance leaves the robot stranded.

KungfuAthleteBot (KAB) resolves these issues systematically. It corrects the aerial phase using laws of physics, initializes exploration from dynamically feasible states, and handles fall recovery seamlessly inside the exact same policy.

sections.heading: Why Have Previous Works Discarded Jumping Motions?
sections.summary: Existing video-based frameworks often discard (filter out) physically inconsistent jump frames, missing the very essence of high-dynamic behavior. Meanwhile, traditional fall recovery has typically been treated as an isolated task or relied heavily on human recovery demonstrations.
sections.details:
Here is how this work fits into the humanoid imitation learning and tracking landscape:

### Data Collection and Learning from Video
MoCap datasets like AMASS provide natural movements but stay mostly in low-to-medium dynamic regimes. VR teleoperation (e.g., TWIST2) and exoskeleton suits capture physically valid data, but the hardware is cumbersome. Prior works using video estimators (like GVHMR)—such as FARM, SONIC, and KungfuBot—frequently mask or discard frames that exceed error thresholds. However, this cuts out the most valuable acrobatic jumps.

### High-Dynamic Tracking and Recovery Control
Methods like BeyondMimic use diffusion models and adaptive sampling, but they struggle with prolonged aerial phases and falls. Conventional stand-up policies (such as HumanUP and HoST) are standalone single-task controllers separate from regular tracking. Recent work like StableMimic unifies tracking and recovery into one policy, but it requires retargeting human recovery MoCap clips. KAB stands apart by learning autonomous recovery using only tracking rewards, without any recovery demonstration data.

sections.heading: Don't Discard Jumps, Fix Them! Physics-Guided Parabolic Correction
sections.summary: The authors created the KungfuAthlete dataset containing extreme athletic motions from 197 videos of Chinese national-level martial artists. They developed a physics-guided correction method that fits free-fall parabolic trajectories to fix aerial floating.
sections.details:
### 3.1 From Raw Video to Robot Trajectories
The authors gathered 197 daily training videos of national-level martial artists and split them into 1,726 clips. Poses were extracted with the monocular estimator GVHMR and retargeted to the 29-DoF Unitree G1 via GMR. The dataset features 822 ground motions and 170 jumping motions, exhibiting significantly higher linear and angular velocities across the whole body than AMASS or LAFAN1. A curated subset of 848 samples is publicly released.

### 3.2 Correcting Root Height Floating and Jitter
Reconstructions from video often suffer from root height 'floating' during the descent phase of jumps. Rather than filtering these out, KAB repairs them through the following pipeline:

- (1) Ground Contact Alignment: Computes the robot's lowest point height $z_{\min}$ and offsets the sequence so the first frame contacts the ground ($z=0$).
- (2) Event Propagation: Identifies local minima of root height as candidate contact events; retains upward motion while suppressing downward drift via velocity integration.
- (3) Ballistic Interpolation: Replaces the descending phase from a local maximum to the subsequent minimum with a free-fall physics model: $\hat{P}(t) = \hat{P}(t_M) - \frac{1}{2}g(t - t_M)^2$.
- (4) Penetration Removal and Smoothing: Pushes up any frames penetrating below the ground ($z < 0$) and applies a Savitzky-Golay filter to eliminate high-frequency jitter.

This turns previously unusable acrobatic jump clips into physically learnable reference trajectories for the robot.

captions.F2: Comparison of jumping and landing motions before (top) and after (bottom) correction. Before correction, the lowest point floats 0.56 m above the ground at landing. After parabolic correction, the feet land cleanly on the ground, forming a physically sound trajectory.

sections.heading: Compensating for Missing Torques: Low-Kinetic-Energy Sampling
sections.summary: Because videos lack torque information, traditional error-driven sampling keeps restarting the policy in physically infeasible states, causing training to fail. To solve this, the authors propose pseudo-low-kinetic-energy (LKE) sampling, which initializes episodes at stable moments of low reference energy.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Why Strict Tracking Fails
Video-derived trajectories are purely kinematic. Because mass distributions and joint torque limits differ between humans and robots, forcing a robot to replicate human joint trajectories demands impossible torque outputs, causing it to fall and halting learning progress.

### 4.2 Pseudo-Low-Kinetic-Energy (LKE) Sampling
Prior imitation learning methods (like BeyondMimic) rely on adaptive sampling, prioritizing frames where the current tracking error is large. However, if the reference trajectory contains aerial poses that are physically infeasible for the robot, error-driven sampling repeatedly picks those impossible frames, failing immediately and stalling training.

To counter this, the authors compute a 'pseudo-kinetic energy' $E_t$ from reference joint velocities, root translation, and angular velocities. They design a softmax distribution that samples frames with lower energy (i.e., near-static, dynamically feasible states) with higher probability. This is LKE sampling. Because it relies only on the physical state of the reference rather than tracking error, the policy starts from stable poses—such as right before a jump or after landing—without wasting resources on impossible aerial poses.

### 4.3 Three-Stage Curriculum Learning
Training follows a three-stage curriculum. Stage I uses relaxed termination criteria to encourage exploration. Stage II tightens tracking bounds and adds penalties for balance and power consumption. Stage III applies severe domain randomization—varying mass, gravity, and applying external pushes—to prepare the policy for sim-to-real transfer.

sections.heading: Recovery Without Demonstrations: A Unified Tracking and Stand-Up Policy
sections.summary: The framework unifies normal motion tracking and fall recovery within the same policy. Without any dedicated recovery reference data, the robot learns to stand up from diverse fallen poses generated by passive gravity drops in about 0.7 seconds.
sections.details:
### 5.1 & 5.2 Unified Reward Design
When operating in the real world, a robot knocked over by a disturbance should recover naturally within its existing controller rather than requiring a manual switch to a separate recovery mode. The unified reward is formulated as a weighted sum of the tracking reward $r_{\mathrm{mt}}$ and the recovery reward $r_{\mathrm{rc}}$.

The transition is driven by the robot's shoulder height error relative to the reference. If the robot falls and deviates by more than a threshold $\tau$, an indicator $\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{recover}}$ activates, shifting priority to the recovery reward (which encourages increasing root height and restoring upright posture).

### 5.3 & 5.4 Gravity-Randomized State Initialization (GRSI)
Instead of using human MoCap recovery data, the authors generate a fallen pose dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{GRSI}}$ in simulation. The robot is set to zero torque and passively dropped under gravity onto floors with varying friction, resulting in prone, supine, lateral, and twisted poses. Initial states are sampled with probability $p$ from standard trajectories and $1-p$ from $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{GRSI}}$ during reinforcement learning (FastSAC), allowing the robot to discover the most natural recovery strategy tailored to its own dynamics.

### 5.5 Grace Period for Early Termination
If an episode terminated immediately upon starting from a fallen pose due to tracking error, learning would never take off. The policy is therefore granted a grace period of 150 consecutive steps (about 3 seconds) where termination conditions are waived during recovery.

captions.F3: Overall training pipeline. Top-left: Low-Kinetic-Energy (LKE) sampling. Bottom-left: Bernoulli mixture initialization between reference trajectories and gravity-dropped fallen states (GRSI). Center: Tracking and recovery rewards with penalty terms. Right: FastSAC reinforcement learning loop running across 8,192 parallel environments.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Experiments: Kung Fu Mastery and a 0.7-Second Stand-Up
sections.summary: Experiments in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1 evaluated dynamic tracking and recovery speed. KAB successfully executes high-dynamic moves that cause prior methods to fail and achieves a recovery time of about 0.7 seconds from arbitrary falls—among the fastest reported for a unified policy.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Benchmark Difficulty Evaluation
Seven challenging athletic motions (running punches, backflips, 360-degree aerial cartwheel kicks, etc.) were evaluated in MuJoCo against representative whole-body controllers (TWIST, GMT, SONIC). Baseline methods consistently fell or broke down during aerial phases and sharp transitions. In contrast, KAB achieved a 100% success rate across all seven motions.

### 6.2 & 6.3 Effects of Curriculum and Sampling
A single-stage BeyondMimic baseline suffered from insufficient exploration on moves like the 360-degree cartwheel, terminating early with rewards plateauing at 7.8. KAB's three-stage curriculum reached 54.6. Furthermore, while adaptive sampling kept restarting at untrackable aerial frames and failed to progress, LKE sampling enabled stable learning of full-length sequences.

### 6.4 Robustness and Recovery Performance
On the physical Unitree G1, the robot was subjected to heavy external pushes while performing a 5-minute Tai Chi sequence. It resisted mild disturbances with stepping and immediately pushed off the ground when knocked down completely. It recovered to an upright stance in about 0.7 seconds across four categories of falls: prone, supine, lateral, and severely tangled limb poses. This is the fastest recovery speed reported among unified tracking policies that do not rely on recovery reference data.

### 6.5 Ablations
Ablations confirmed that adding recovery rewards does not degrade tracking precision, omitting the grace period causes training to fail instantly, and both height and root orientation rewards are strictly required for stable stand-up behaviors.

captions.F5: Recovery sequences from diverse fallen states. Top four rows show simulation results (prone, supine, and two complex twisted limb poses); bottom two rows show real-robot trials on the Unitree G1. The robot smoothly pushes against the floor and stands up regardless of the initial collapsed pose.

sections.heading: Moving from Merely Collecting Video to Repairing and Compensating It
sections.summary: Learning extreme humanoid motions from video demands repairing physical errors, compensating for missing actuation, and integrating failure recovery. Simply collecting more data is not enough; conditioning data with physical principles is key.
sections.details:
This study systematically resolved the fundamental obstacles (C1–C3) in learning advanced humanoid motor skills from video. Through physics-guided parabolic correction for aerial trajectories, LKE sampling and curricula for missing torques, and a reference-free unified recovery policy, the physical humanoid mastered acrobatic skills while acquiring the resilience to stand up from arbitrary falls in ~0.7 seconds.

The authors conclude that scaling up raw video collection alone cannot unlock high-dynamic skills. Instead, repairing data using physical laws and compensating for missing dynamics via intelligent reinforcement learning is the crucial breakthrough.

sections.heading: Appendix: Additional Acrobatic Skills and Network Details
sections.summary: Details on the network architecture, reward functions, and additional simulated acrobatic motions—such as a 720-degree aerial spin into a kick—are summarized here.
sections.details:
### Rewards and Network Architecture
The actor and critic networks use 3-layer ELU MLPs with hidden dimensions of (512, 256, 128). Built on BeyondMimic, the reward places a heavy weight on tracking whole-body angular velocity. This prioritizes overall dynamic rotational momentum over overfitting to exact individual joint angles.

### Additional Acrobatic Motions
In addition to the motions discussed in the main text, simulation results confirm the robot stably executes extreme stunts, such as a 720-degree aerial spin followed immediately by a 360-degree kick upon landing (Motion 78), as well as dynamic lateral breakfalls and rolls (Motion 1480).

captions.F7: Acrobatic stunt (Motion 78) acquired in simulation. The robot executes a 720-degree mid-air spin, lands, and seamlessly unleashes a 360-degree kick, demonstrating remarkable stability through extreme, non-stationary dynamics.

takeaways: When extracting motions from video, repairing trajectory errors using physical laws like parabolic gravity models preserves valuable high-dynamic jumps that threshold filtering normally discards.
When imitating trajectories that lack torque information, error-driven restarts trap the robot in infeasible aerial poses; initializing from low-kinetic-energy (LKE) states enables stable learning.

Human demonstration data is not necessary for fall recovery. Reinforcement learning on passive, gravity-dropped fallen states lets the robot discover an ultra-fast recovery strategy (~0.7 s) tailored to its own hardware.
Tracking and fall recovery do not require separate controllers; they can be unified in a single policy using a multitask reward switched by simple metrics like shoulder height deviation.
limitations: Detecting contact candidate points (local minima) in the parabolic correction pipeline still involves some manual annotation for ambiguous cases, falling short of a fully automated end-to-end system.
While recovering in ~0.7 seconds is advantageous for sports and martial arts, the extreme motor stress and torque spikes present safety trade-offs in shared human environments.
Physical testing was performed exclusively on a single platform (Unitree G1); generalizing across humanoid robots with different masses and kinematic link structures remains to be validated.
